newsitem.title: CHINA: China stocks mostly up, ignoring official warning.
newsitem.headline: China stocks mostly up, ignoring official warning.

text.p: China's stock investors on Monday ignored a new official warning on market volatility, and share prices ended generally higher in sharp contrast to falls sparked by a similar caution last December.
Analysts said they were somewhat puzzled by the warning from Beijing's securities authorities, published in all the main financial newspapers.

"For one thing, the markets aren't overheated," said an analyst with one foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "Last December, they were posting unsustainable volumes and price rises. That is not the case now."
"In only three months, the Shanghai stock market has risen nearly 40 percent and the Shenzhen market more than 40 percent," an editorial in Monday's China Securities newspaper said.
"Compared with China's overall economic development, the markets have displayed signs of overheating."
Despite the warning, Shanghai's A share index rose 1.24 percent to close at 1,338.058 points on Monday, while the B share index ended up 0.59 percent at 73.925 points.
In Shenzhen, the A share index closed up 1.07 percent at 468.99 points, although the B index lost 0.53 percent to 160.41 points.

After a sudden bout of speculative activity towards the end of last year, the official People's Daily, mouthpiece of the Chinese Communist Party, issued a stern warning to investors that the markets were overheating.
The market indices dropped around 30 percent in response, but have since clawed back all the lost ground with steady gains over the past three months.
Stock analysts said prices were supported by the prevailing expectation that China's economy would continue to improve this year with the performance of listed firms moving in tandem.
"Investors ignored the warning largely because market fundamentals have improved greatly in recent months," said an executive with a major Chinese brokerage.
"The national economy continues to show signs of further improvement this year and listed firms' results are expected to be much better," he added.
Analysts said that while prices were high, the fundamental mood of the Chinese markets was different from the hothouse days of early December.

"The recent gains on the stock markets contrast sharply with the rises last year," said one trader. "The price structure of the markets has changed given the strong gains by blue-chip companies. This is no longer pure speculation in the stocks of poorly-performing firms."

Analysts predicted that if 1997 interim reports confirmed the expectations of an upturn in listed firms' business, share prices on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchange would hit new highs again in August or September.

"Unless the central government takes further and concrete measures to force the markets down, share prices will continue to rise with only periodically technical corrections for the rest of this year," said one stock analyst.
